title: ZICA Zambia
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public ZICA syllabus (financial accounting, management accounting, taxation, audit). Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.stem: A machine is acquired for K240,000 with an estimated useful life of six years and a residual value of K30,000. Using the straight-line method, what is the annual depreciation charge?
items.explanation: Straight-line depreciation is cost minus residual value divided by useful life, so 240,000 minus 30,000 equals 210,000, divided by six years gives K35,000. Ignoring the residual value would wrongly give K40,000.

items.stem: A trader holds inventory costing K80,000. Its estimated selling price is K72,000 and the estimated costs to complete the sale are K5,000. Under IAS 2, at what amount should the inventory be carried?
items.explanation: Net realisable value is the selling price less costs to complete, so 72,000 minus 5,000 equals 67,000. IAS 2 requires the lower of cost and net realisable value, so 67,000 is used rather than the 80,000 cost.

items.stem: A building with a carrying amount of K500,000 is revalued to K590,000. Under the revaluation model in IAS 16, how should the surplus of K90,000 be treated?
options: Recognised immediately in profit or loss as income
Deducted from the cost of the building in the ledger
Recognised in other comprehensive income and accumulated in equity as a revaluation surplus
Deferred and recognised over the asset's remaining useful life
items.explanation: An upward revaluation is taken to other comprehensive income and accumulated in equity as a revaluation surplus, not to profit or loss. A reversal of a previous revaluation loss would instead be recognised in profit to the extent of that loss.

items.stem: Which set of conditions must all be met before a provision is recognised under IAS 37?
options: A future operating loss is expected and management approves the amount
The obligation is only possible rather than probable and is disclosed instead
A board resolution has been passed even though no external obligation exists
A present obligation from a past event, a probable outflow of resources and a reliable estimate
items.explanation: IAS 37 requires a present obligation arising from a past event, a probable outflow of economic benefits and a reliable estimate before a provision is recognised. A merely possible obligation is a contingent liability disclosed in the notes rather than provided for.

items.stem: Under IFRS 15, at what point is revenue from a contract with a customer recognised?
options: When the entity satisfies a performance obligation by transferring a promised good or service
When the customer places a firm order
When cash is received from the customer
When the written contract is signed by both parties
items.explanation: IFRS 15 recognises revenue when control of the promised good or service transfers to the customer as a performance obligation is satisfied. The timing of cash receipt or contract signature does not by itself determine revenue recognition.

items.stem: Under IFRS 16, how does a lessee initially measure the right-of-use asset?
options: At the total undiscounted lease payments over the whole lease term
At the initial lease liability adjusted for payments made at or before commencement, initial direct costs and restoration costs
At the fair value of the underlying asset on the commencement date
At the sum of the first year's lease payments only
items.explanation: The right-of-use asset starts at the initial lease liability plus amounts paid at or before commencement, initial direct costs and estimated restoration costs. Using undiscounted payments would overstate the asset and ignore the time value of money.

items.stem: In a statement of cash flows prepared under IAS 7, how may interest paid by a non-financial entity be classified?
options: Only within investing activities
Only within financing activities
Either within operating or within financing activities applied consistently
Only within operating activities
items.explanation: IAS 7 permits interest paid to be classified as either operating or financing, provided the choice is applied consistently. It may not be shown in investing activities or switched freely from period to period.

items.stem: After the reporting date but before the financial statements were approved, a company learned that inventory held at the year end had been sold below cost. Under IAS 10, how should this be treated?
options: As a non-adjusting event disclosed only in the notes
Ignored entirely because it occurred after the year end
Recognised as a prior period error against opening retained earnings
As an adjusting event because it provides evidence of conditions that existed at the reporting date
items.explanation: Evidence that inventory was worth less than cost at the reporting date confirms a condition existing at that date, so it is an adjusting event and the inventory is written down. Non-adjusting events merely indicate conditions arising after the reporting date.

items.stem: An asset costs K160,000 and is depreciated at 25 percent per year on the reducing balance method. What is the depreciation charge for the second year?
items.explanation: First-year depreciation is 160,000 times 25 percent, which is 40,000, leaving a carrying amount of 120,000. Second-year depreciation is 120,000 times 25 percent, which is K30,000, because the reducing balance applies to the written-down value.

items.stem: A business paid K18,000 during the year for insurance, of which K3,000 relates to the following year. Under the accruals basis, what is the insurance expense for the current year?
items.explanation: The amount relating to the next year is a prepayment and must be removed, so 18,000 minus 3,000 equals K15,000 of expense. Charging the full 18,000 would breach the accruals and matching principles.

items.stem: At 31 December a firm's bank statement showed a credit balance of K25,000. Cheques drawn but not yet presented were K4,000 and a receipt of K2,000 was banked but not yet credited. What is the adjusted cash book balance?
items.explanation: Starting from the bank statement balance of 25,000, deduct unpresented cheques of 4,000 and add the deposit not yet credited of 2,000, giving K23,000. Unpresented cheques reduce the balance while deposits in transit increase it.

items.stem: An asset has a carrying amount of K90,000, a fair value less costs of disposal of K70,000 and a value in use of K75,000. Under IAS 36, what are the recoverable amount and the impairment loss?
options: Recoverable amount of K70,000 and an impairment loss of K20,000
Recoverable amount of K90,000 and no impairment loss
Recoverable amount of K75,000 and no impairment loss
Recoverable amount of K75,000 and an impairment loss of K15,000
items.explanation: The recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use, so it is 75,000. The impairment loss is the carrying amount minus the recoverable amount, so 90,000 minus 75,000 equals K15,000.

items.stem: Under IFRS 9, how should a company measure the loss allowance for trade receivables that do not contain a significant financing component?
options: At an amount equal to lifetime expected credit losses
At an amount equal to twelve-month expected credit losses only
At the full gross carrying amount of the receivables
At the amount of debts known to be uncollectible at the year end
items.explanation: IFRS 9 requires a simplified approach for trade receivables without a significant financing component, measuring the loss allowance at lifetime expected credit losses. Twelve-month expected credit losses apply to some other financial assets.

items.stem: A company issues 100,000 ordinary shares of K1 each at a premium of K0.50 per share. How should the proceeds of K150,000 be recorded?
options: Share capital of K150,000 and no share premium
Share capital of K100,000 and share premium of K50,000
Share capital of K50,000 and share premium of K100,000
Share capital of K100,000 and retained earnings of K50,000
items.explanation: The nominal value credited to share capital is 100,000 shares times K1, which is K100,000, and the excess of the issue price over nominal value is share premium of 50,000. Share premium is a capital reserve and is not part of retained earnings.

items.stem: A company declares a final dividend after the reporting date but before the financial statements are approved for issue. Under IAS 10 and IAS 1, how is the dividend treated at the reporting date?
options: It is recognised as a current liability at the reporting date
It is recognised as a prior period adjustment
It is not recognised as a liability but is disclosed in the notes
It is deducted from the revaluation surplus
items.explanation: A dividend declared after the reporting date does not represent an obligation at that date, so it is not recognised as a liability and is instead disclosed in the notes. Recognising it as a liability would understate equity and overstate liabilities.

items.stem: Under IAS 2, which cost is excluded from the cost of inventory and instead recognised as an expense when incurred?
options: The cost of purchase including import duties
Conversion costs that convert materials into finished goods
Transport costs incurred in bringing inventory to its present location
Abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour or other production costs
items.explanation: IAS 2 excludes abnormal waste from the cost of inventory, so it is expensed when incurred. Purchase costs, conversion costs and inward transport are all included in the cost of inventory.

items.stem: Under IAS 38, how is expenditure incurred during the research phase of an internally generated intangible asset treated?
options: It is recognised as an expense when incurred
It is capitalised as an intangible asset
It is carried as a deferred asset until the project succeeds
It is offset against the revaluation surplus
items.explanation: IAS 38 prohibits capitalising research expenditure because future economic benefits cannot yet be demonstrated, so it is expensed when incurred. Development expenditure may be capitalised only once the specified recognition criteria are met.

items.stem: Under IAS 7, which item qualifies as a cash equivalent?
options: A trade receivable due within sixty days
A short-term highly liquid investment with insignificant risk of change in value
Inventory held for resale within the operating cycle
An equity investment held for long-term capital growth
items.explanation: Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible to known amounts of cash with insignificant risk of change in value. Receivables, inventory and long-term equity investments do not meet this definition.

items.stem: A trial balance extracted from the ledgers fails to agree. Which type of error would cause the trial balance to disagree?
options: Posting a payment to the wrong expense account
Recording a transaction twice with equal debits and credits
Recording only one side of a double entry
Compensating errors that offset each other
items.explanation: An error of omission of one side of a double entry leaves the debit and credit totals unequal, so the trial balance disagrees. Wrong-account postings, duplicate entries and compensating errors keep the totals equal.

items.stem: A partnership agreement entitles a partner to an annual salary of K60,000. How should this salary be treated in the partnership financial statements?
options: As an operating expense in arriving at profit for the year
As a liability recognised only when paid in cash
As a distribution deducted from share capital
As an appropriation of profit rather than an operating expense
items.explanation: Under IAS 10 and partnership accounting, partner salaries and interest on capital are appropriations of profit, not expenses of the business. Treating them as expenses would misstate the profit available for appropriation.

items.stem: A product sells for K40 per unit with a variable cost of K25 per unit. Annual fixed costs are K120,000. What is the break-even point in units?
options: 8,000 units
4,800 units
3,000 units
12,000 units
items.explanation: Contribution per unit is 40 minus 25, which is K15. Break-even units equals fixed costs divided by contribution, so 120,000 divided by 15 equals 8,000 units. Dividing fixed costs by the selling price would wrongly give 3,000 units.

items.stem: Using the same product, current sales are 10,000 units while the break-even point is 8,000 units. What is the margin of safety in units?
options: 10,000 units
2,000 units
8,000 units
18,000 units
items.explanation: The margin of safety is actual sales minus break-even sales, so 10,000 minus 8,000 equals 2,000 units. It measures how far sales can fall before the business makes a loss.

items.stem: Fixed costs are K90,000, the contribution per unit is K18 and the target profit is K36,000. How many units must be sold to achieve the target profit?
options: 2,000 units
5,000 units
7,000 units
9,000 units
items.explanation: Required units equals fixed costs plus target profit divided by contribution per unit, so 90,000 plus 36,000 equals 126,000, divided by 18 gives 7,000 units. Using fixed costs alone would give the break-even of 5,000 units.

items.stem: A machine hour is the single scarce resource and two products both use it. Which basis should be used to rank the products for production?
options: Contribution per unit
Selling price per unit
Total fixed cost absorbed per unit
Contribution per machine hour
items.explanation: When a resource is limited, products should be ranked by contribution earned per unit of the limiting factor, here contribution per machine hour. Ranking by contribution per unit ignores how much of the scarce resource each product consumes.

items.stem: A manager is deciding whether to accept a one-off special order. Which cost is irrelevant to the decision?
options: A sunk cost already incurred on a feasibility study
The incremental materials needed for the order
The additional labour hours required for the order
The opportunity cost of using spare capacity elsewhere
items.explanation: A sunk cost has already been incurred and cannot be changed by the decision, so it is irrelevant. Incremental materials, additional labour and opportunity costs are all future costs that differ between alternatives.

items.stem: The standard is 5 kilograms of material at K4 per kilogram. Actual production used 4,800 kilograms purchased at K4.20 per kilogram. What is the material price variance?
options: K960 favourable
K960 adverse
K800 adverse
K1,200 adverse
items.explanation: The price variance is the standard price minus the actual price multiplied by actual quantity, so 4.00 minus 4.20 equals negative 0.20, times 4,800 gives K960 adverse. Paying more than standard makes the variance adverse.

items.stem: The standard allows 5 kilograms per unit and 1,000 units were produced. Actual usage was 4,800 kilograms and the standard price is K4. What is the material usage variance?
options: K800 adverse
K960 favourable
K800 favourable
K4,000 favourable
items.explanation: Standard usage for actual output is 5,000 kilograms. The usage variance is 5,000 minus 4,800 equals 200 kilograms favourable, multiplied by the standard price of K4 gives K800 favourable. Using less material than standard is favourable.

items.stem: The standard labour rate is K12 per hour. Actual hours worked were 2,100 at a rate of K12.50 per hour. What is the labour rate variance?
options: K1,050 favourable
K1,200 adverse
K1,000 adverse
K1,050 adverse
items.explanation: The rate variance is the standard rate minus the actual rate multiplied by actual hours, so 12.00 minus 12.50 equals negative 0.50, times 2,100 gives K1,050 adverse. A rate above standard produces an adverse variance.

items.stem: Budgeted overhead is K300,000 and budgeted labour hours are 60,000, giving an absorption rate of K5 per hour. Actual hours were 62,000 and actual overhead was K305,000. What is the overhead over or under absorption?
options: K5,000 over absorbed
K5,000 under absorbed
K10,000 over absorbed
K5,000 under absorbed at K10 per hour
items.explanation: Overhead absorbed is 62,000 hours times K5, which is K310,000, against actual overhead of K305,000. Because absorbed exceeds actual, overhead is over absorbed by K5,000.

items.stem: Annual demand is 20,000 units, the cost of placing an order is K50 and the holding cost per unit per year is K2. Using the economic order quantity formula, what is the order size?
options: 500 units
1,000 units
2,000 units
100 units
items.explanation: The economic order quantity is the square root of two times demand times order cost divided by holding cost, so 2 times 20,000 times 50 divided by 2 equals 1,000,000, whose square root is 1,000 units. This minimises total ordering and holding costs.

items.stem: A process inputs 5,000 units and a normal loss of 10 percent is expected with no scrap value. How many good units are expected to be output?
options: 500 units
5,000 units
4,500 units
4,000 units
items.explanation: Normal loss is 10 percent of 5,000, which is 500 units, so expected good output is 5,000 minus 500 equals 4,500 units. The normal loss cost is absorbed by the good units produced.

items.stem: At 8,000 units total cost is K34,000 and at 5,000 units total cost is K25,000. Using the high-low method, what is the variable cost per unit?
items.explanation: The variable cost per unit is the change in cost divided by the change in activity, so 34,000 minus 25,000 equals 9,000, divided by 3,000 units gives K3.00. The fixed cost is then 34,000 minus 3 times 8,000, which is K10,000.

items.stem: A project costs K100,000 and generates equal annual cash inflows of K25,000. What is the payback period?
options: 4.0 years
3.0 years
5.0 years
2.5 years
items.explanation: Payback is the initial outlay divided by the annual cash inflow, so 100,000 divided by 25,000 equals 4.0 years. Payback ignores cash flows after the payback date and the time value of money.

items.stem: A project requires an initial investment of K100,000 and generates average annual profit after depreciation of K20,000. What is the accounting rate of return?
options: 5 percent
20 percent
80 percent
25 percent
items.explanation: The accounting rate of return is average annual profit divided by the initial investment, so 20,000 divided by 100,000 equals 20 percent. It uses accounting profit rather than cash flow and ignores the time value of money.

items.stem: A Zambian company reports taxable profits of K800,000 and the corporate income tax rate is 30 percent. What is the income tax charge for the year?
items.explanation: Income tax is the taxable profit multiplied by the tax rate, so 800,000 times 30 percent equals K240,000. The after-tax profit is therefore K560,000.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: A registered supplier sells standard-rated goods for K116,000 inclusive of value added tax at 16 percent. What is the output VAT?
items.explanation: Where the price is VAT inclusive, output VAT is the total multiplied by the tax fraction 16 divided by 116, so 116,000 times 16 over 116 equals K16,000. The net value of the supply is K100,000.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: A company buys plant for K200,000 and claims a capital allowance at 25 percent per year on the reducing balance. What is the allowance for the first year?
items.explanation: The first-year allowance is the cost multiplied by the rate, so 200,000 times 25 percent equals K50,000. The reducing balance then applies 25 percent to the written-down value in later years.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: A person transfers land with a realised value of K500,000 and property transfer tax is charged at 5 percent. What is the property transfer tax payable?
items.explanation: Property transfer tax is the realised value multiplied by the rate, so 500,000 times 5 percent equals K25,000. The tax is a transfer tax on the value of the property transferred.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: A company pays a dividend of K200,000 to a resident shareholder and withholding tax on dividends is charged at 15 percent. What is the withholding tax?
items.explanation: Withholding tax is the dividend multiplied by the rate, so 200,000 times 15 percent equals K30,000. The company deducts the tax and remits it to the revenue authority on behalf of the shareholder.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: A small business has annual turnover of K600,000 and is taxed under turnover tax at 4 percent of turnover. What is the turnover tax payable?
items.explanation: Turnover tax is the turnover multiplied by the applicable rate, so 600,000 times 4 percent equals K24,000. Turnover tax is based on gross turnover rather than taxable profit.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: Which expense is generally disallowed when computing a company's taxable business income?
options: Depreciation of plant and machinery charged in the accounts
Salaries and wages paid to employees
Rent paid for business premises
Interest paid on a business loan
items.explanation: Accounting depreciation is disallowed because capital expenditure is relieved through capital allowances instead. Salaries, business rent and loan interest are generally deductible if incurred wholly and exclusively for the business.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: Which supply is treated as zero-rated for value added tax purposes?
options: The supply of standard-rated goods to a local retailer
The export of goods to a customer outside the country
The supply of exempt financial services
The supply of goods by a business not registered for VAT
items.explanation: Exports are zero-rated, which means VAT is charged at 0 percent and input tax may still be recovered. Exempt supplies carry no VAT and generally block input tax recovery.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: A offers to sell his car to B for K50,000. B replies that he will buy it for K45,000. What is the legal effect of B's reply?
options: It is an unqualified acceptance of the original offer
It is a mere request for information with no legal effect
It is a counter-offer that destroys the original offer
It creates a binding contract at K45,000
items.explanation: A reply that varies the terms of an offer is a counter-offer, which rejects and destroys the original offer. The original offer can no longer be accepted unless A renews it.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: Which statement best describes the rule of consideration in a simple contract?
options: Consideration must always be adequate in money terms
Past consideration is always sufficient consideration
Consideration is not required where an offer has been made
Consideration must be of some value and must not be past
items.explanation: Consideration must have some value in the eyes of the law and must be given in return for the promise, so past consideration is generally insufficient. The law does not require consideration to be adequate, only sufficient.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: A contract is made between A and B for the benefit of C, who is not a party to it. Under the doctrine of privity of contract, what is C's position?
options: C cannot enforce the contract because C provided no consideration
C can enforce the contract because C benefits from it
C becomes a party automatically on signing the contract
C can enforce the contract only if A agrees
items.explanation: Privity of contract means only the parties to a contract can enforce it, and consideration must move from the promisee, so C cannot sue on the contract. Exceptions exist where statute or the arrangement grants C enforceable rights.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: An agent enters into a contract that is beyond the authority actually granted by the principal. Under what circumstances may the principal still be bound?
options: Where the agent personally believes the act is authorised
Where the principal ratifies the act or the agent acted within apparent authority
Where the third party knew the agent lacked authority
Where the contract is oral rather than written
items.explanation: A principal may be bound by an unauthorised act if the principal ratifies it or if the agent acted within apparent authority created by the principal. A third party who knows the agent lacks authority cannot rely on apparent authority.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: In a general partnership, what is the liability of each partner for the debts of the firm?
options: Limited to the amount of capital each partner contributed
Limited to the amount shown in the partnership agreement
Unlimited joint liability, so personal assets are at risk
No personal liability because the firm is a separate person
items.explanation: In a general partnership the partners have unlimited liability for the debts of the firm and are jointly liable, so their personal assets may be used to settle firm debts. A limited liability partnership or company limits this exposure.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: Under a contract for the sale of goods by description, which implied term applies to the goods supplied?
options: The goods must be fit for every conceivable purpose
The seller must always provide the goods free of charge
The buyer must inspect the goods before delivery
The goods must correspond with the description given
items.explanation: Where goods are sold by description, it is an implied term that the goods correspond with that description. A separate implied term requires fitness for a particular purpose only where that purpose is made known to the seller.
items.reference: ZICA Syllabus - Taxation and Business Law

items.stem: Audit risk comprises inherent risk, control risk and detection risk. Which component can the auditor directly influence?
options: Detection risk
Inherent risk
Control risk
All three components equally
items.explanation: Detection risk is a function of the effectiveness of the auditor's procedures and can be reduced by doing more or better work. Inherent risk and control risk belong to the entity and are assessed rather than controlled by the auditor.

items.stem: How is materiality best described in the context of an audit of financial statements?
options: The exact amount of every misstatement found during the audit
An amount that could influence the economic decisions of users taken on the financial statements
A fixed percentage of revenue applied to all entities
The total value of the entity's assets at the year end
items.explanation: Materiality is the threshold at which misstatements could reasonably influence the economic decisions of users. It is a matter of professional judgement and is not a fixed percentage.

items.stem: Which procedure is most appropriate for obtaining evidence about the existence of a client's inventory?
options: Reviewing the prior year's depreciation schedule
Confirming the bank balance directly with the bank
Attending the physical inventory count and performing test counts
Inspecting the minutes of a shareholder meeting
items.explanation: Attendance at the physical count and performing test counts provides direct evidence about existence and condition of inventory. Bank confirmations address cash, not inventory, and the other procedures are irrelevant to inventory existence.

items.stem: What is a primary purpose of the auditor obtaining an understanding of the entity's internal control?
options: To guarantee that all fraud will be detected
To express an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control
To replace substantive testing with control testing entirely
To identify risks of material misstatement and design further audit procedures
items.explanation: Understanding internal control helps the auditor identify and assess risks of material misstatement and design the nature, timing and extent of further procedures. An audit opinion is on the financial statements, not on internal control effectiveness.

items.stem: Under ISA 570, what is the auditor's responsibility in relation to going concern?
options: To obtain sufficient appropriate evidence about the appropriateness of management's use of the going concern basis
To guarantee that the entity will remain in business for the next year
To prepare the cash flow forecast on behalf of management
To ignore going concern where the entity made a profit
items.explanation: The auditor must obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence regarding management's use of the going concern assumption and conclude whether a material uncertainty exists. The auditor does not guarantee survival or prepare management's forecasts.

items.stem: The auditor concludes that the possible effects of a misstatement in the financial statements are both material and pervasive. Which opinion should be expressed?
options: A qualified opinion
An adverse opinion
An unmodified opinion with an emphasis of matter paragraph
An unmodified opinion with no modification
items.explanation: When misstatements are material and pervasive the auditor expresses an adverse opinion because the financial statements as a whole are not fairly presented. A qualified opinion is used when the effect is material but not pervasive.

items.stem: The auditor identifies a misstatement in inventory that is material but not pervasive. The rest of the financial statements are fairly stated. Which opinion is appropriate?
options: An adverse opinion
A disclaimer of opinion
A qualified opinion
An unmodified opinion with no modification
items.explanation: A material but not pervasive misstatement leads to a qualified opinion, described in a basis for qualified opinion paragraph. An adverse opinion is reserved for material and pervasive misstatements.

items.stem: Under ISA 240, what primarily distinguishes fraud from error?
options: The monetary value of the misstatement
Whether the misstatement was found by the auditor or by management
The account balance in which the misstatement arises
Whether the action that caused the misstatement was intentional
items.explanation: The distinguishing feature of fraud is intent, that is whether the misstatement arose from an intentional act to deceive. Error is an unintentional misstatement, regardless of its size.

items.stem: Which behaviour best reflects an attitude of professional scepticism by an auditor?
options: Questioning contradictory evidence and remaining alert to possible misstatement
Assuming that management is always dishonest
Accepting management's explanations without corroboration
Relying solely on oral representations as audit evidence
items.explanation: Professional scepticism means questioning evidence and being alert to conditions that may indicate misstatement, without assuming management is either dishonest or honest. Accepting explanations without corroboration undermines scepticism.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of an audit engagement letter?
options: To provide the auditor's opinion on the financial statements
To document the agreed terms of the engagement and avoid misunderstanding
To replace the need for a written audit plan
To confirm that all fraud has been eliminated
items.explanation: The engagement letter records the agreed terms, the scope of the audit and the respective responsibilities of the auditor and management, reducing the risk of misunderstanding. The audit opinion is issued later in the auditor's report.

items.stem: Under ISA 560, what should the auditor do if facts become known after the date of the audit report that might have caused a revision of the report?
options: Ignore the facts because the audit is complete
Withdraw the audit opinion without any communication
Discuss the matter with management and take the action required by the standard
Amend the financial statements personally
items.explanation: ISA 560 requires the auditor to discuss the matter with management and, where the financial statements are amended, perform necessary procedures and report accordingly. Ignoring the facts would breach the standard.

items.stem: Under ISA 530, which factor most directly increases the sample size the auditor needs to select?
options: An increase in the tolerable misstatement
A decrease in the assessed risk of material misstatement
An increase in the amount of audit evidence already obtained
A decrease in the tolerable misstatement
items.explanation: A lower tolerable misstatement means the auditor needs a larger sample to detect misstatements that matter, all else being equal. Raising tolerable misstatement or lowering assessed risk allows a smaller sample.
